mcqs.question: What's the honest limit of any thread-safety test, according to the answer skeleton?
options: Tests can only prove a class is thread-safe if they run for at least 24 hours continuously
Tests are only valid if they use exactly 100 threads
Tests can only be trusted if written in the same language as the class under test
No test can prove the absence of a race — it can only fail to reproduce one on the runs it happened to perform
mcqs.explanation: Races are timing-dependent, so a passing test only tells you those specific runs didn't hit a bad interleaving, not that none exists. There's no such 24-hour rule, no fixed thread-count requirement, and language matching has nothing to do with test validity.

mcqs.question: Why does the CountDownLatch-based stress test surface races more reliably than simply starting N threads independently?
options: It forces every thread to reach a starting line and then releases them all at the same instant, maximizing genuine overlap instead of relying on staggered OS thread-start timing
It reduces the number of threads needed to trigger any race to exactly two
It disables the JVM's garbage collector during the test run
It guarantees the race will be reproduced on every single run
mcqs.explanation: The ready/start latch pair synchronizes every thread's launch, producing far more genuine simultaneous execution than threads starting whenever the OS scheduler happens to run them. It doesn't fix the thread count at two, doesn't touch garbage collection, and still can't guarantee reproduction on every run.

mcqs.question: What can code review catch that a stress test fundamentally cannot?
options: Code review can measure the exact CPU time a lock is held under production load
A reviewer can identify a check-then-act or read-modify-write pattern by inspection, without depending on scheduling luck to actually trigger a visible failure
Code review can automatically rewrite unsafe code into a thread-safe equivalent
Code review guarantees 100% detection of every race in a codebase
mcqs.explanation: A human reading for the pattern doesn't need the bug to actually manifest under some specific timing, unlike a test. Review doesn't measure runtime lock-hold time, doesn't auto-rewrite code, and isn't a guarantee of catching every race — it depends on the reviewer noticing the pattern.

mcqs.question: Why is claiming a passing stress test "proves" a class is race-free an overstatement?
options: Because stress tests are not permitted in most production codebases
Because stress tests can only be run on single-core machines
A stress test samples a small, effectively random slice of possible thread interleavings, not an exhaustive one, so passing runs are evidence, not proof
Because a stress test always modifies the class under test to make it artificially pass
mcqs.explanation: Passing runs only show that the specific interleavings sampled didn't trigger a failure — the full space of possible schedules is far larger and mostly unsampled. Stress tests are common in production codebases, run fine on multi-core machines, and don't modify the class under test.
